title: How many people lived in the Americas in 1491?
summary: Estimates range from 8 to 112 million; many scholars now cluster around 45-60 million. The answer sets the scale of the collapse that followed.
why: It sets the scale of the demographic catastrophe after European contact.

notes.problem: Page gives Dobyns 'possibly over 100 million' (1960s), not '90-112 million (1966)'; 'widely questioned' overstates 'multiple researchers have called ... into question'.

question: How many people lived in the Americas just before European contact in 1492?
evidence: Kroeber (1939) estimated 8.4 million, Dobyns (1960s) possibly over 100 million, Denevan about 54 million; a 2018 carbon-record study gave just over 60 million; a 2020 genetic study suggests Caribbean estimates may be tenfold too high.
wouldSettle: Independent regional evidence, from archaeology, ancient DNA and environmental records, converging on the same totals.

theories.name: Low counts
theories.idea: Kroeber's 8.4 million; such figures often reflected notions of European superiority.

theories.name: High counts
theories.idea: Dobyns, from historical and archaeological data, possibly over 100 million; multiple researchers question such high figures.

theories.name: Middle consensus
theories.idea: Denevan's 'consensus count' of about 54 million; most newer estimates fall between 45 and 60 million.
